Contrastive alignment depends on useful positive and negative comparisons, and adaptive fusion can only help if the available views contain complementary signal. The reported experiments use real-world datasets, but the abstract does not specify domain types, failure cases, privacy costs, serving cost, or how the method behaves when language descriptions are wrong, biased, stale, or missing.

458.bp: The ordinary problem is not a map problem in the abstract; it is a government work-planning problem. Taiwan has to define legal land boundaries, and that requires field teams to go out, inspect parcels, and complete boundary demarcation work. If managers cannot estimate how long each field task will take, they cannot assign staff well, balance workloads fairly, or plan capacity from evidence instead of habit. The paper serves that operating system: a web platform that predicts fieldwork duration and helps visualize scheduling choices. The object being predicted is time needed for real surveying work, not merely a score in a model table. The available clues come from two kinds of records: spatial information about where tasks sit and tabular information about task properties. SAMPLE asks how those clues can be combined so land offices can move from an unstructured planning pipeline to a data-driven scheduling system.
458.wh: The hard part is that fieldwork duration is shaped by several uneven sources of evidence. A parcel's location matters because nearby or connected tasks can share geographic difficulty, local conditions, or operational patterns. But location alone is not enough, because ordinary task records may contain non-spatial details that also affect duration. Time may matter in repeated cycles, so a plain date or task order can hide periodic patterns. Workload fairness adds another pressure: a wrong forecast is not just a prediction error; it can send too much work to one team and too little to another. A model that treats every spatial neighbor as equally useful may spread misleading evidence. A model that treats every feature column as equally useful may drown out the few columns that explain the current case. The system therefore has to decide which place-based clues and which tabular clues deserve influence for each prediction.
458.naive: A smart beginner might start with a spreadsheet. They would average the durations of past land-boundary jobs, perhaps split by district, and use that average to schedule the next batch. A more technical beginner might train a standard tabular predictor on the available task columns and ignore the map except as a location code. Both ideas fail for the same reason: they flatten the work. Nearby tasks may reveal shared field conditions, but a district average is too coarse. Tabular columns may matter differently in different places, but a single global rule treats them as fixed. The result is inaccurate duration forecasting, poor task allocation, and workload imbalance, which are exactly the failures the abstract says conventional processes suffer from.
458.ap: SAMPLE's central move is to treat each field task as something described by both its place in a spatial structure and its ordinary recorded attributes, then let the system learn how much each kind of evidence should count. The graph component treats land-boundary work as connected cases rather than isolated rows. The periodic encoding gives repeated time patterns a usable numerical form instead of leaving them as raw calendar values. The multilayer perceptron handles the tabular side: it learns relationships among ordinary feature columns. Spatial and channel-wise attention are weighting mechanisms: they assign different influence to different places and different information channels before the final duration estimate is made. The web platform wraps this prediction engine in a system for scheduling, forecasting, and visualization, so the output can support resource planning rather than sit as an offline experiment.
458.mech: The mechanism begins with past land-boundary demarcation records. Each record supplies a target to learn from: how long fieldwork took. It also supplies inputs: spatial data and tabular data. The spatial data is organized as a graph, meaning tasks or places are treated as points, and connections describe which points may carry useful evidence for one another. The graph convolution part lets a task revise its internal description using information from connected tasks. That is useful only if the system controls whose evidence matters, so spatial attention assigns stronger weight to more relevant neighboring structure and weaker weight to less relevant structure. In parallel, the tabular features pass through a multilayer perceptron, a stack of learned transformations that turns raw columns into a prediction-ready description. Periodic linear encoding changes repeating time signals into a form where cycles can be learned rather than mistaken for simple one-way growth. Channel-wise attention then weighs different feature channels, so a location clue, a repeated time clue, and a tabular clue do not all speak equally by default. These transformed pieces are combined into a duration forecast. The platform then uses the forecast in a web-based scheduling and visualization system. The paper evaluates this combined architecture against XGBoost, TabPFN, TabNet, and GCN plus MLP baselines, and also compares the platform with a conventional unstructured pipeline.
458.math: The first mathematical idea is learning a function from examples: use past jobs with known durations to learn a rule that turns a new job's evidence into a duration estimate. The rule is not hand-written because the relation between place, task attributes, repeated timing, and field duration is too tangled for a simple checklist. The second idea is graph reasoning. A graph is a map of items and links; here the items are spatially situated land-boundary tasks or places, and links mean that evidence may travel between related locations. The risk is that links can mislead, so the third idea is weighted combining, called attention in the model name. A weight is a number saying how loudly one neighbor or one feature channel should speak in the final prediction. The fourth idea is periodic encoding: repeated patterns are represented so the model can notice cycles instead of treating time as only a straight line. The final idea is error reduction: the model's controllable settings are adjusted so predicted durations move closer to observed durations. The core tradeoff is local detail versus shared structure: borrow from connected tasks and repeated patterns, but do not let irrelevant neighbors or columns overpower the current case.
458.dots: This paper sits in the time-series and spatiotemporal family because the answer depends on both where work happens and how patterns repeat over time. It is a sibling of traffic, city activity, sensor, and service-health papers in the repo's current taxonomy: each must preserve spatial relationships and temporal structure before making a forecast. It also connects to graph learning because it assumes connected places can carry evidence about one another. The conference-wide attention idea appears here in a practical form: not every neighbor and not every feature channel deserves equal trust. SAMPLE also touches efficiency and public-sector decision support. Unlike retrieval or recommendation papers, it is not choosing documents or items for a user; it is estimating labor time so scarce field teams can be allocated more fairly. The broader pattern is the same, though: a real system has too much uneven evidence, and the model must learn which pieces should influence the next decision.
458.ww: The method should improve over the naive approach because it matches the shape of the evidence more closely. A spreadsheet average can say what usually happened, but it cannot express that one task should borrow heavily from certain nearby tasks and lightly from others. A plain tabular model can learn from columns, but it may miss the fact that land work is spatial: adjacent or related areas can reveal conditions that a row of numbers does not fully state. A graph model can borrow across locations, but without careful weighting it may spread weak or irrelevant signals. SAMPLE combines these strengths. The graph component lets place-based evidence travel. The spatial weighting limits that travel to the parts that look useful. The channel weighting keeps one information source from dominating every case. The periodic encoding lets recurring patterns be reused. The multilayer tabular component still captures ordinary feature relationships. If past records contain repeatable connections among location, task attributes, calendar-like cycles, and duration, the combined system has more chances to find those relationships than any single-source baseline.
458.po: The payoff is a practical planning capability for land administration. Instead of relying on an unstructured pipeline, the office gets a web-based system for field-task scheduling, duration forecasting, and visualization. The abstract reports that the proposed model outperforms XGBoost, TabPFN, TabNet, and GCN plus MLP baselines in multiple experiments and ablation studies. It also reports up to an 88 percent reduction in time and labor costs compared with the conventional unstructured data pipeline. Grounded in the abstract, the main benefit is better forecasting and scheduling support, which can improve task allocation, workload balance, and data-driven resource planning.
458.limits: The abstract does not prove that the same system will work outside Taiwan's land-boundary demarcation setting, or under different legal, geographic, staffing, and data-recording practices. The approach assumes that historical records are accurate enough, that spatial links genuinely carry useful evidence, and that repeated time patterns continue to matter. If field procedures change, if a rare task type appears, or if the graph connects places that do not share operational difficulty, the learned weights can become confident about the wrong evidence. The abstract reports comparisons and ablation studies, but it does not detail the dataset size, deployment duration, fairness metrics for workload distribution, or failure cases where the forecast remains unreliable.

459.bp: A biomedical lab is a place where small physical mistakes can matter: a liquid can spill, a pipette can touch the wrong surface, a hand can block a safe motion, and a container that looks harmless may be partly full. An autonomous lab agent therefore needs more than a label saying beaker, glove, or bottle. It needs a usable picture of what can be grasped, poured, avoided, or queried. WPIS starts from ordinary web images of lab activity, because those images show real handling situations rather than carefully staged scans. The paper asks whether a single uncalibrated image can be turned into a structured record that a reasoning system can inspect. The goal is a physics-aware 3D scene graph: objects become entries, relations say how they sit and interact, liquid states become numbers, and hand-object actions become smaller linked structures. That record gives a language model something cleaner than raw pixels when answering feasibility and safety questions.
459.wh: The hard part is that web photos are useful precisely because they are uncontrolled. They usually come from one camera view, with no camera calibration, no measured camera settings, no second view, and no known 3D model of the lab equipment. A person can often infer that one vessel is behind another or that a hand is holding a tube, but the image itself does not directly give exact distances, volumes, or forces. Standard 3D reconstruction methods are built for settings where the camera, scene, or object shapes are more controlled. Simple object recognition also stops too early: it may find a flask and a hand, but it does not say whether the flask is partly filled, whether the hand is aligned with the object, or what operation is physically possible. WPIS has to bridge the gap between messy two-dimensional evidence and the queryable physical knowledge that an autonomous lab system needs for precise object and liquid handling.
459.naive: A smart beginner might give the lab photo directly to a strong vision-language model and ask questions such as whether a pouring action is safe or which object the hand is using. That can work for obvious labels, but it forces the model to do everything at once: detect objects, infer depth, guess liquid state, track hand-object contact, and reason about safety. Another beginner might first run a detector and store only object names and boxes. That also fails because boxes do not explain functional relations. A container above another, a hand touching a tool, and a visible liquid level are not just visual details; they are the evidence that decides whether an action is feasible. Without an explicit structure, the reasoning system must repeatedly rediscover these relations from pixels.
459.ap: WPIS turns a single lab image into an intermediate object that is closer to how a careful technician would describe the scene. It first gathers open-vocabulary instance and mask cues, meaning it tries to find named objects and their visible outlines without being limited to a tiny fixed label list. It then adds relative geometry, which is not a perfect measurement of meters but an ordering and approximate shape of where things sit in depth. The graph nodes represent scene entities, and the links represent spatial, physical, and functional relations. The paper adds two lab-specific details that plain scene graphs often miss: real-valued liquid states for containers, and fine-grained hand-object interaction subgraphs that spell out which hand is doing what to which object. It also attaches short natural-language functional relations, so the resulting graph can answer not only what is present but what actions the scene appears to allow.
459.mech: The mechanism begins with one RGB image from the web. WPIS looks for visible lab objects and separates their pixels into masks, so each item has an outline rather than only a rough rectangle. From the same image it estimates relative depth, giving a proxy for which surfaces and objects are nearer or farther even though the camera is not calibrated. It then compiles these signals into a physics-aware 3D scene graph. In that graph, each node stands for an object or relevant part of the scene; node attributes store information such as object identity, spatial position, and, for containers, a real-valued liquid state rather than a vague full-or-empty label. The system also builds hand-object interaction subgraphs. These smaller structures connect hands, objects, and action-like relations so that a query can distinguish a hand near a tool from a hand actually aligned with or using it. WPIS attaches concise language descriptions of functional relations, such as relations that matter for object and liquid handling. The output is paired with relative depth and a single-image point-cloud proxy in the WebLab-3DSG knowledge base. A language model can then answer by reading the structured graph, instead of relying only on raw image impressions.
459.math: The main mathematical idea is structured representation: take a flat image and rewrite it as a set of named parts plus relations among those parts. A graph is the natural shape for this because lab reasoning is about connected facts. The nodes are things such as vessels, tools, hands, and liquids; the links say how those things are placed, touched, or functionally related. Relative geometry supplies ordered spatial evidence when exact measurement is unavailable. It answers questions like nearer versus farther or above versus below, accepting that the numbers are approximate but still useful. Segmentation, the act of separating the image into object-shaped regions, is a comparison problem: each pixel is assigned to the object whose visual evidence fits best. Liquid state is treated as a real-valued attribute, so the graph can carry degrees rather than only categories. The single-image point-cloud proxy is a compressed 3D guess: it preserves enough surface layout to reason about placement while admitting that one image cannot recover the full scene. The tradeoff is detail versus usability. WPIS gives up exact reconstruction, but gains a queryable structure that makes physical relations explicit.
459.dots: This paper sits where multimodal vision-language work, knowledge graphs, and agent reasoning meet. Like other multimodal papers, it is trying to align visual evidence with words, but its center of gravity is action: the important question is not merely whether the image contains a container, but whether a lab agent can safely use it. Like knowledge-graph papers, it treats relations as first-class evidence rather than decoration. The graph format matters because a later question can follow links among hands, objects, liquid states, and functional descriptions. It also connects to retrieval-augmented reasoning for language models: instead of asking a model to reason directly from pixels, the system supplies a structured scene record as grounding. Compared with ordinary scene understanding, WPIS adds physical affordances and safety constraints. Compared with full 3D capture systems, it accepts weak web-image evidence and tries to make that evidence operational.
459.ww: The approach works when weak clues become stronger together. A mask alone says where an object appears. Relative depth alone says something about front and back. A hand-object relation alone says something about use. Liquid state alone says something about possible pouring or spilling. None of these clues is enough to support reliable lab reasoning by itself, but a graph can keep them in one place and make their dependencies visible. That helps a language model because the model no longer has to search the image for every needed fact during every question. It can inspect a prepared record: which object is involved, where it sits, whether it contains liquid, how a hand relates to it, and what function is described. The reported expert study supports this intuition: grounding a language model in the physics-aware scene graph improves answer quality by 40 percent over a strong vision-language model that reasons directly from RGB, with especially large gains on feasibility, hand-object alignment, and safety constraints.
459.po: The payoff is a practical path from ordinary web imagery to lab-useful physical reasoning. WPIS releases WebLab-3DSG, a 1,000-scene knowledge base in which each RGB image is paired with a physics-aware scene graph JSON, relative depth, and a single-image point-cloud proxy. That turns scattered online lab images into structured examples that can be queried and studied. For autonomous laboratory systems, the important gain is not prettier image understanding but better answers about what can be done safely and feasibly. The abstract reports a 40 percent answer-quality improvement when a language model uses the graph rather than reasoning directly from the image.
459.limits: The abstract does not prove that the recovered 3D structure is metrically precise, and the method explicitly works without camera settings, multiple views, or known 3D object models. Its claims therefore depend on relative geometry and visual cues being good enough for the intended reasoning questions. Web images may omit crucial context outside the frame, hide liquid levels, or show unusual lab tools that detectors handle poorly. Natural-language functional relations also depend on whether the pipeline describes the real affordance rather than a plausible but wrong one. The expert study shows improved answer quality, but the abstract does not establish safe real-world robotic execution from these graphs alone.

460.bp: Federated learning is useful when many devices or organizations each hold private examples, but nobody wants to gather all records in one central place. In edge computing, those holders are often phones, sensors, small machines, or local servers with very different abilities. Some can train deep classification models; others cannot afford that much computation, memory, or repeated communication. This paper serves the practical need to learn one useful global classifier from that mixed population without forcing every client to act like the strongest machine. The ordinary system problem is coordination under uneven resources: the server needs useful knowledge from everyone, but weak clients cannot keep joining many training rounds. FedMHO is aimed at that setting. It combines model-heterogeneous federated learning, where clients may use different model types or sizes, with one-shot federated learning, where clients communicate only once or almost once. The paper asks how to make that limited exchange still produce a strong global model.
460.wh: The hard part is that the usual federated recipe assumes repeated negotiation. Each client trains locally, sends an update, receives a new shared model, trains again, and repeats. That loop is costly even when clients have similar hardware. It becomes unfriendly when some clients are resource-constrained and cannot run large classifiers or communicate many times. One-shot learning reduces communication, but then the server gets only a small amount of evidence from each client. Model heterogeneity helps weak devices use smaller models, yet it creates another mismatch: the server cannot simply average unlike models as if they had the same shape and meaning. Existing methods, according to the abstract, either get unsatisfactory global model performance or rely on auxiliary datasets. The auxiliary-data requirement is a serious practical weakness because a server may not have a public dataset that matches the private client data. FedMHO must therefore solve three tensions at once: limited rounds, unequal client capacity, and no extra central data.
460.naive: A smart beginner might ask every client to train the largest shared classifier it can, send the final model once, and let the server average the received parameters. That fails for this paper's setting because the weakest clients may not be able to train the large classifier at all. If the server allows different model sizes, direct averaging no longer makes sense because the parts do not line up. Another beginner move is to ignore weak clients and learn from resource-sufficient clients only, but then the global model loses data patterns that exist on constrained devices. A third move is to use a public auxiliary dataset for distillation, meaning teaching one model from another through shared examples, but the abstract says reliance on auxiliary datasets is one of the problems FedMHO tries to avoid.
460.ap: FedMHO's central move is to change what weak clients send. Instead of asking every client to send the same kind of classifier, it lets resource-sufficient clients use deep classification models and resource-constrained clients use lightweight generative models. A generative model is a small machine for producing example-like samples rather than directly making the final classification decision. This reframes one-shot federated learning as a two-stage server task. First, the server uses what the constrained clients provide to generate synthetic samples, meaning artificial examples intended to reflect the local data patterns those clients saw. Second, the server performs knowledge fusion, combining what the stronger classification models know with the generated evidence from weaker clients. The key practical idea is that a weak device can contribute by describing how its data looks, not by training the same heavy classifier as everyone else. The paper then adds variants, FedMHO-MD and FedMHO-SD, to reduce knowledge forgetting during fusion.
460.mech: The mechanism starts with a population of heterogeneous edge clients. Each client has local data, but clients differ in available computation and communication capacity. Resource-sufficient clients train deep classification models on their own data. These models carry decision knowledge: which input patterns tend to belong to which classes. Resource-constrained clients instead train lightweight generative models. Their contribution is not a full heavy classifier but a compact way to produce samples resembling their local data. In the one-shot setting, clients send their trained model objects or summaries to the server without the usual long cycle of repeated update exchanges. The server then runs the first stage, data generation. It asks the lightweight generators to produce synthetic samples so the missing client data can be represented without copying raw private records. The abstract also says FedMHO uses an unsupervised data optimization solution to improve synthetic sample quality. In plain terms, because the server may not have labels or an auxiliary dataset for checking every generated sample, it must adjust the generated examples using internal criteria that make them more useful for learning. The second stage is knowledge fusion. The server uses synthetic samples and the knowledge from deep classification models to form a global model. During this stage, FedMHO-MD and FedMHO-SD are introduced to mitigate knowledge forgetting, the risk that while absorbing one source of knowledge the global model loses useful behavior from another source. The output is a global classifier intended to reflect both strong and constrained clients.
460.math: The main mathematical idea is constrained information sharing. Each client has useful evidence, but raw examples should stay local and weak clients cannot afford the same training burden as strong clients. FedMHO therefore asks what smaller object can cross the boundary while still preserving useful class patterns. For strong clients, the object is a classification model, which maps inputs to class decisions. For constrained clients, the object is a generative model, which represents a recipe for drawing sample-like inputs. Generation is a form of approximation: instead of moving the original data points, the system tries to recreate the shape of the local data well enough for training. Knowledge fusion is a second mathematical move: several imperfect sources are combined into one model. This resembles teaching by examples and teacher behavior, where the global model is adjusted so its outputs agree with useful signals coming from client models and generated samples. The phrase optimization appears in the abstract for synthetic data quality; here it means defining what makes a generated sample useful and adjusting controllable choices to reduce bad samples without labels. The tradeoff is privacy and communication cost versus detail. Synthetic samples and small generators save resources, but they can distort rare local patterns. Fusion also creates a stability tradeoff: learning new client knowledge must not overwrite already absorbed knowledge.
460.dots: This paper sits inside the repo's privacy, federated, and security family because it asks what useful signal may cross a device boundary without centralizing raw data. It is close to RAFed, which also deals with federated learning on non-identical clients while trying to lower communication cost, but FedMHO's sharper pressure is model heterogeneity plus one-shot communication. It is also close to PAECL and FedBridge in the current repo data: those papers handle edge or model-heterogeneous collaboration by creating shared summaries, aligning knowledge, or using distillation-like transfer rather than pretending every client has the same model. The broader conference connection is to optimization and information compression. Many papers must decide what to keep when full evidence is too expensive to move. FedMHO's answer is to keep decision behavior from strong clients and sample-producing recipes from constrained clients. Its sibling problem is not only privacy; it is fair participation when weaker devices still hold data that the global model should learn from.
460.ww: The approach should improve over the naive one because it matches each client's job to its capacity. A resource-sufficient client can afford a deep classifier, so it contributes rich decision knowledge. A constrained client may not be able to train or transmit that kind of model, but it can still learn a lightweight generator that captures part of its local data shape. That keeps weak clients from being excluded. The server-side generation step gives the fusion process concrete training material, so the global model is not forced to combine incompatible model parameters directly. This matters because different model architectures may encode knowledge in different internal forms; samples provide a more common meeting ground. The unsupervised data optimization step is meant to reduce the damage from low-quality synthetic samples, which would otherwise teach the global model misleading patterns. The forgetting-mitigation variants address another reason fusion can fail: as the server absorbs knowledge from one source, it can drift away from knowledge learned from another. FedMHO works if generated samples preserve enough of each constrained client's useful data structure and if the fusion stage can balance client signals instead of letting one source dominate.
460.po: The payoff is a federated learning setup better suited to real edge deployments where clients are uneven. Grounded in the abstract, FedMHO aims to reduce communication pressure through one-shot federated learning, handle different client resources through model heterogeneity, avoid reliance on auxiliary datasets, and still produce a stronger global model. Its practical capability is letting constrained clients contribute through lightweight generative models while stronger clients contribute through deep classification models. The abstract reports comprehensive experiments and says the methods outperform state-of-the-art baselines across several experimental settings, so the claimed benefit is not just lower communication but better global model performance under the mixed-client design.
460.limits: The abstract does not specify the datasets, model architectures, privacy guarantees, or exact criteria used for unsupervised synthetic data optimization, so those details cannot be inferred here. FedMHO assumes constrained clients can still train useful lightweight generative models. If their generators are poor, biased, or miss rare classes, the synthetic samples may mislead the server. It also assumes generated samples are safe enough from a privacy standpoint, but the abstract does not prove that they cannot leak sensitive local patterns. One-shot communication reduces cost but leaves little chance to correct bad client contributions. The reported experiments support effectiveness in tested settings, not every edge deployment with extreme hardware, data imbalance, or adversarial clients.

461.bp: A DAG-based blockchain is a shared transaction machine. Instead of arranging every transaction in one strict line, it lets many blocks point to earlier blocks in a directed acyclic graph: a one-way web where history does not loop back on itself. That shape promises more parallel work, which matters for decentralized finance, Internet-of-Things devices, and distributed applications that cannot wait for a slow global queue. The practical problem is that speed does not come from the graph shape alone. The system has knobs at several layers: how nodes talk, how consensus decides what is accepted, how execution work is scheduled, and how the graph grows. Alzo serves operators who need the chain to keep high throughput and low latency while traffic changes. The paper treats blockchain operation less like installing a fixed protocol and more like running a live control system whose settings must respond to workload pressure.
461.wh: The hard part is that the blockchain's knobs do not act independently. A network setting that sends information more aggressively may help consensus see new blocks sooner, but it may also increase communication load. A consensus setting that accepts work quickly may reduce waiting time, but it can affect graph shape and later execution. A graph-topology choice that improves parallelism under one workload may create extra coordination under another. Manual configuration fails because the operator sees a moving target: traffic rises and falls, nodes observe different local conditions, and the best setting for one stage may be harmful when another stage is congested. A single flat learner would also face a huge search space. It would have to discover which layer caused a slowdown, which parameter can influence that layer, and which temporary improvement is safe enough to apply to a live chain.
461.naive: A smart beginner would pick a few fixed configurations, run load tests, and deploy the one with the best average throughput and latency. If traffic later changes, they might tune one obvious parameter by hand, such as making consensus faster or changing how the graph expands. That approach fails because the best average setting can be the wrong live setting. A quiet workload, a burst of DeFi transactions, and many small IoT updates can stress different parts of the system. One-knob repairs are also risky because the layers are coupled. The beginner may fix the visible symptom, such as waiting time, while creating a hidden problem in communication load, execution backlog, or graph structure.
461.ap: Alzo's central move is to turn configuration into staged learning from feedback. Reinforcement learning means the tuner tries an action, observes a reward or penalty, and gradually prefers actions that repeatedly lead to better outcomes. The paper makes that idea hierarchical: instead of asking one policy to control every blockchain knob at once, it decomposes the DAG workflow into distinct stages. Stage-level metrics tell the tuner where the system is hurting and which family of parameters should be adjusted. The policy then controls critical settings for consensus, execution, and graph topology in real time. The other central move is safety. A shadow-control loop checks parameter changes before they affect the real system, so Alzo can learn and adapt without treating production infrastructure as an unprotected experiment.
461.mech: The input to Alzo is a running DAG-based blockchain plus measurements from its workflow. The abstract names stage-level performance metrics, so the relevant signals are things like how much work the chain finishes, how long transactions wait, and where pressure appears across consensus, execution, and graph-topology stages. First, Alzo separates the workflow into those stages instead of flattening the whole chain into one undifferentiated machine. Second, each stage exposes controllable parameters: consensus choices govern agreement behavior, execution choices govern how accepted work is processed, and graph-topology choices govern how blocks or references shape the DAG. Third, the hierarchical policy reads the current measurements and chooses adjustments at the proper level. A higher-level decision can decide which stage needs attention, while lower-level decisions choose the concrete parameter changes inside that stage. Fourth, the system scores the result by whether throughput rises, latency falls, and overhead remains small under the current workload. Fifth, the shadow-control loop acts as a guardrail. Before a proposed setting reaches the live chain, the controller can evaluate or screen it outside the main control path. The output is not a new block or transaction; it is a continuously updated configuration policy that steers the chain as workload conditions vary.
461.math: The main mathematical idea is sequential decision-making under feedback. The tuner does not know the best configuration in advance, and the value of a setting can only be judged after the system responds. Reinforcement learning is the plain-language loop of choosing an action, seeing a score, and updating future choices so actions with better repeated scores become more likely. Hierarchy matters because the action space is too large if every parameter is chosen in one flat list. Breaking the workflow into stages creates smaller decision problems that match the system's physical structure: consensus, execution, and graph topology each have their own local symptoms and controls. The score is an optimization target, meaning a rule for what counts as better: more completed work, less waiting, and little added overhead. The graph idea also matters. A DAG is a network of blocks with one-way references, so topology parameters change how evidence about transaction order and validity spreads through that network. The key tradeoff is exploration versus safety. The learner needs to try new settings to discover better behavior, but a blockchain cannot tolerate reckless trials. The shadow-control loop is therefore a mathematical and engineering constraint: it narrows action choices to those that appear safe enough before they touch the live system.
461.dots: This paper sits in the repo's optimization and reinforcement-learning families. The shared pressure is too many possible choices for hand rules and a world that changes while the system is running. It is close to DeFi arbitrage work, advertising budget allocation, networked-control papers, and cloud quality-of-service systems because all of them define a score, observe feedback, and adjust scarce resources or settings under constraints. It also connects to network reasoning. DAG blockchains are not isolated records; their behavior depends on how nodes and blocks are connected and how information moves through those connections. Compared with blockchain security papers in the current data, Alzo is less about detecting misuse or preserving privacy and more about operational control: keeping decentralized infrastructure fast without breaking consensus behavior. Its sibling idea is adaptive systems design, where the method must improve speed while respecting safety, overhead, and live deployment pressure.
461.ww: Alzo should help because it matches the shape of the problem. A DAG blockchain has staged causes of delay, so a staged controller has a better chance of assigning blame than a single global rule. If latency rises because execution is backed up, changing graph topology may not help; if graph growth creates coordination pressure, only speeding execution may miss the bottleneck. Stage-level feedback gives the learner a clearer error signal. Over repeated workloads, the policy can learn which parameter changes tend to reduce the measured pain in each stage. The hierarchical split also reduces wasted search: the system does not need to test every possible cross-layer combination equally often when the current metrics point to a narrower region. The shadow-control loop addresses the reason many adaptive controllers are scary in infrastructure. It lets Alzo evaluate a candidate adjustment before applying it, so learning can proceed while limiting harmful live actions. The result is a controller that can react faster than manual tuning while staying more disciplined than blind trial and error.
461.po: The payoff is an auto-tuned DAG blockchain that adapts to variable workloads without a human repeatedly rewriting configuration files. The abstract reports higher throughput and lower latency than other configurations, with minimal overhead. In practical terms, the chain can process more work and make users wait less while traffic patterns change. That matters for decentralized finance, Internet-of-Things traffic, and distributed applications because these systems become unpleasant or unsafe when confirmation delay rises during bursts. Alzo buys a live steering layer for blockchain performance rather than a one-time best setting chosen in advance.
461.limits: The claims depend on the stage decomposition matching the real bottlenecks of the target DAG blockchain. If important behavior crosses stages in ways the controller cannot observe, stage-level metrics may point to the wrong cause. The reinforcement learner also needs feedback that is frequent and honest enough to separate a real improvement from a lucky workload fluctuation. The shadow-control loop reduces risk, but the abstract does not prove that every unsafe parameter interaction can be detected before deployment. The experiments show better throughput and latency under variable workloads, yet the abstract does not specify how broadly those workloads represent production chains, adversarial conditions, node churn, or economic incentives.

462.bp: This paper is about a very ordinary but high-stakes web moment: a person sees a health claim and must decide whether it is true enough to trust. The claim may concern a treatment, a risk, or a public-health recommendation, so a wrong judgment can shape real behavior outside the browser. The authors are not building a detector that reads the claim for the user. They are studying how users themselves check claims while using the web. The central contrast is between looking outward across several sources and staying inside a smaller set of pages for longer. The first behavior is lateral reading; the second is vertical reading. The study asks whether the outward move helps people detect health misinformation, and whether it still helps when the claim agrees with what the person already tends to believe. The useful object is therefore not only the final true-or-false judgment, but the browser behavior that led there.
462.wh: The hard part is that fact-checking is partly invisible. A platform can see whether someone clicked, switched tabs, or spent time away, but it cannot easily see the private reasoning that happened in the user's head. Time alone is also ambiguous. A person may spend a long time carefully comparing evidence, or they may simply reread a misleading page until it feels familiar. Belief makes the problem harder. When a health statement matches a user's attitude, the user may feel less need to inspect it, and this confirmation bias can make false claims feel already settled. The study also has to separate individual differences from the behavior being measured. Some participants may be generally better at judging claims, some claims may be easier, and some topics may attract stronger prior attitudes. The challenge is to test whether the checking strategy itself is linked to accuracy rather than mistaking personality, topic, or chance for an effect.
462.naive: A smart beginner might say: just tell users to spend more time reading before they decide. That sounds reasonable because careful reading feels like the opposite of snap judgment. But health misinformation often lives inside a page that is internally persuasive. More time with one source can deepen trust in the same weak evidence instead of exposing its weakness. Another beginner move would be to ask users afterward whether they fact-checked. That fails because self-reports are noisy: people forget, overstate effort, or describe what they think they should have done. The paper instead treats observable navigation as evidence of the checking strategy, then asks which strategy actually predicts better detection.
462.ap: The paper's core move is to turn fact-checking from a vague mental activity into measurable browser behavior. Lateral reading becomes a pattern of moving outside the starting interface, especially switching tabs or windows to consult other sources. Vertical reading becomes spending more time on fewer sources. The experiment gives 1,842 participants health-related statements inside a purpose-built web platform and logs behavioral signals while they judge whether the material is misinformation. Then the analysis compares detection accuracy with these behaviors. It also tests whether the benefit changes when the statement's valence aligns with the user's attitude, which is the paper's operational way to capture confirmation bias. The striking result is directional and practical: lateral reading is associated with higher accuracy, vertical reading is not, and the lateral-reading benefit is not weakened by the measured attitude alignment.
462.mech: The mechanism begins with a participant facing a health-related claim in the experimental web setting. The participant can stay near the presented material or leave the interface to check elsewhere. While this happens, the platform records signals such as tab or window switches and time spent outside the interface. These signals are not treated as perfect mind reading. They are treated as traces of different verification habits: many outward moves suggest cross-source checking, while extended dwell time without such movement suggests deeper reading of fewer sources. After the participant gives a misinformation-detection answer, the study has three important pieces of information for that case: the answer's accuracy, the navigation pattern, and whether the claim's valence fits the participant's attitude. The analysis then compares many such cases across 1,842 people. Linear mixed-effects models, meaning statistical comparisons that can account for repeated observations and uneven differences among people or items, estimate the relationship between behavior and accuracy. Semiparametric bootstrap confidence intervals, meaning repeated resampling used to judge how stable the estimate is without assuming a perfectly simple error shape, provide uncertainty around the result. The output is not an automatic fact-check label; it is evidence that tab-switch-style lateral checking is a reliable sign of better health-misinformation judgment.
462.math: The main mathematical idea is comparison under uncertainty. The study cannot replay each person's private reasoning, so it compares observable traces with final accuracy across many repeated cases. A linear mixed-effects model asks a plain question: after allowing for the fact that people and claims can differ, does one behavior tend to move accuracy up or down? The fixed part of the model estimates the average link between a strategy and correctness. The mixed part allows some variation to belong to participants or statements, rather than forcing every difference to be explained by lateral or vertical reading. The reported beta for lateral reading is positive, meaning more of that behavior is associated with higher accuracy; the vertical-reading estimate is near zero and not statistically convincing. The confidence interval is a range of estimates that remain plausible after accounting for sampling noise. The p-value asks how surprising a result this strong would be if there were no real relationship in the studied setting. The moderation test asks a different mathematical question: does attitude alignment change the slope between lateral reading and accuracy? The reported result says the study did not find such a change.
462.dots: This paper belongs in the misinformation-trust family because it treats trust as an evidence process, not as a label attached to a single page. Many neighboring papers in the repo build machine systems that retrieve evidence, judge source support, calibrate confidence, or produce verification reports. This one studies the human version of the same deeper move: leave the original claim, gather outside evidence, and let disagreement across sources challenge first impressions. It connects to retrieval because lateral reading is a human search strategy: the user chooses where to look next and which outside information deserves attention. It connects to probability because the study estimates how much confidence to place in a behavioral cue such as tab switching. It also connects to causality-aware work in a cautious way: the abstract reports an experimental study and statistical association, while the explanation still depends on whether the logged behavior really captures the verification action that improves judgment.
462.ww: The reason lateral reading should help is that many false health claims can sound complete when inspected alone. A single page can have confident language, selective evidence, or familiar framing. Moving across sources changes the information shape. The user is no longer asking whether one page feels convincing; they are asking whether independent sources tell the same story. That creates more chances for a false claim to collide with missing support, contradictory wording, or more reliable outside context. Vertical reading does not necessarily create that collision. It may only give the same source more time to shape the user's sense of plausibility. The result about confirmation bias matters because attitude alignment is exactly where one might expect cross-checking to fail: if the claim agrees with the user's view, outside search might become performative or selective. The paper finds that the measured lateral-reading benefit remains, suggesting that the physical act of opening other sources can add useful friction even when the user's starting attitude points toward belief.
462.po: The payoff is practical. The study gives web platforms and digital-literacy efforts a simple target: encourage users to open other sources, not merely to spend longer on the same material. It also identifies a scalable behavioral cue. Tab-switch frequency and time outside the experimental interface can indicate verification quality without requiring a platform to inspect private thoughts or ask users to self-report. Grounded in the abstract, the result is strongest for health misinformation detection in the studied online experiment: lateral reading improves accuracy, vertical reading does not, and measured confirmation bias does not erase the lateral-reading advantage.
462.limits: Several assumptions matter. Tab or window switching must usually mean useful outside checking, not distraction or unrelated browsing. The standalone experimental platform must be close enough to ordinary web behavior for the result to transfer. The health claims, participant pool, and attitude measure may not cover all topics, cultures, devices, or misinformation campaigns. The abstract reports that confirmation bias did not moderate the relationship, but that depends on defining bias as alignment between statement valence and user attitude. The study shows a behavioral association in an experiment; it does not prove that every platform nudge to open another tab will improve real-world decisions.

463.bp: The ordinary problem is a harmful spread that has already happened: a rumor moves through social accounts, malware travels across machines, or a disease-like signal appears across connected places. The responder sees the current traces and wants to know where the first push came from. That source matters because stopping spread is not only about treating the visible affected nodes; it is also about understanding the route by which damage entered the network. This paper serves that need by treating source finding as a backward reconstruction problem. Instead of asking only which node looks most central or most infected, it asks which starting point, if allowed to flow through the observed network over real time, could have produced the observed propagation pattern. The title names continuous time because real spread is not naturally a stack of neat rounds. A message, infection, or cascade can move at irregular moments, and those timing traces are evidence.
463.wh: The hard part is that the observer has two imperfect objects at once: the propagation record and the network through which the propagation moved. The record has timing information, but many older source-localization methods flatten time into discrete steps, as if spread happens at round one, round two, and round three. That loses the gradual shape of real movement. The network itself is also noisy. A listed link may be irrelevant, weak, outdated, or accidental, while an important route may be hidden inside a complicated topology. Graph neural network based localization models aggregate information from neighbors, but aggregation is only helpful when neighbors carry trustworthy evidence. If a model gathers signals through noisy links, the wrong parts of the graph can speak too loudly. The central tension is therefore backward inference under bad plumbing: the method must reverse a spreading process while avoiding false clues created by messy graph structure.
463.naive: A smart beginner might score each node by simple clues: infected early-looking neighborhoods, number of connections, distance to observed infected nodes, or how well a short discrete simulation from that node matches the final state. This can work in clean toy networks, but it breaks in the setting described by the abstract. First, real propagation is continuous, so forcing it into fixed time bins can hide who led whom. Second, high-degree or centrally placed nodes may look guilty just because noisy topology lets many irrelevant signals aggregate around them. Third, a local score may miss global propagation habits, such as common flow directions or network-wide patterns. The beginner method confuses visible reach with origin and treats all structural links as equally useful evidence.
463.ap: The paper's central move is to model spreading forward as a flowing dynamical system, then solve source localization as the inverse version of that system. In plain terms, it builds a machine that can say, 'if this were the starting condition, here is how the spread would continuously change over time,' and then uses that machine backward to infer the likely source. The proposed SNODE combines three pieces. One piece is a neural ordinary differential equation, which means a learned rule for how the propagation state changes from one instant to the next. A second piece is a graph variational autoencoder based neural process, which compresses global propagation patterns into a conditioning signal for that change rule. A third piece is spectral graph filtering, which smooths away high-frequency graph components that the abstract says degrade aggregation. The result is not just a node scorer; it is a time-aware inverse model.
463.mech: The input is a real-world propagation case: a graph describing who can influence whom or where spread can travel, together with observations of the propagation over continuous time. The method first imagines the forward process. At every instant, each node has a propagation state, and a learned change rule says how those states should flow through the network as time passes. That is the ODE part: it represents change by a local rate rather than by a fixed jump between snapshots. Then the model needs broader context, because a single cascade is easier to interpret when the system knows what global propagation patterns tend to look like. The graph variational autoencoder based neural process encodes those global patterns into a hidden conditioning variable, a compact summary that guides the ODE system. Before relying on graph aggregation, the method performs spectral graph optimization. This views the graph through frequency-like components: smooth, low-frequency structure corresponds to broad agreement across connected areas, while high-frequency components often mark abrupt, noisy variation. The model filters out the high-frequency parts that damage aggregation quality. Finally, source localization becomes inverse ODE modeling: compare which possible source conditions, passed through the learned continuous-time flow and conditioned on global patterns, best explain the observed propagation. The output is the inferred source.
463.math: The main mathematical idea is an inverse dynamical problem. A dynamical system is a rule for how something changes over time; here the changing object is the propagation state across graph nodes. An ordinary differential equation expresses change as a rate: instead of saying 'after one step, jump here,' it says 'at this moment, this is the direction and speed of change.' That fits continuous-time spread because the timing of movement carries information. The inverse part means the paper observes later evidence and asks what starting source would make the forward flow produce it. The graph supplies the shape of possible movement: nodes are entities, links are possible transmission routes, and aggregation means collecting evidence from neighbors. The risk is that links can lie, so the paper also uses spectral graph reasoning. Spectral methods rewrite graph variation into smooth and jagged components, like separating broad motion from local static. Filtering high-frequency components is a way of suppressing abrupt topology noise before neighbor information is combined. The variational autoencoder adds probability-flavored compression: it summarizes global propagation patterns as a hidden variable while acknowledging that many detailed histories could explain limited observations. The tradeoff is detail versus useful signal: keep enough timing and network structure to infer the source, while removing noise that would make the backward explanation unstable.
463.dots: This paper sits at the meeting point of graph reasoning, sequences over time, probability, and source localization. It shares the graph-learning pressure seen across the conference: relationships are useful because neighbors can carry evidence, but real networks are noisy, so raw link-following can amplify mistakes. It also connects to time-series and spatiotemporal work because the ordering and spacing of events matter, not merely the final set of affected nodes. The inverse modeling angle is close to causal reconstruction: the paper is not only predicting what happens next, but asking what earlier cause could have generated the observed later pattern under a learned forward rule. Its spectral filtering connects to a broader family of methods that smooth, compress, or denoise structure before learning from it. The neighboring idea is that useful models often need two maps at once: a map of where evidence can travel and a map of which parts of that travel map should be trusted.
463.ww: The method should beat the naive approach because it preserves the evidence that source finding naturally depends on. If two candidate sources lead to the same final infected set but one would have produced the observed timing more naturally, a continuous-time flow can distinguish them while a coarse discrete method may not. If a candidate source looks plausible only because noisy edges connect it to many affected nodes, spectral filtering can reduce that false support before aggregation happens. The conditioning variable from the graph variational autoencoder based neural process also helps because a local cascade snapshot is ambiguous by itself. Global propagation patterns can tell the ODE system which kinds of spread are typical in this network setting and which explanations are less coherent. In everyday terms, the model listens to three kinds of evidence together: when the spread happened, where the graph says movement is possible, and which graph patterns look reliable after noise is suppressed. A source that explains all three is more convincing than a node that merely has many infected neighbors.
463.po: The payoff is a more realistic way to identify the origin of harmful propagation in continuous-time scenarios. The abstract reports that SNODE outperforms the best baseline in real-world continuous-time propagation settings with an average performance improvement of 43.8%, and it also says the method achieves consistently superior performance under noisy topology. Practically, that means the system is meant for cases where investigators cannot assume clean links or neat time steps. It buys a stronger source estimate by turning timing, graph structure, global propagation habits, and denoising into one inference process rather than treating them as separate afterthoughts.
463.limits: The claim depends on the forward ODE model being a good enough description of the actual spread. If real propagation changes because of outside interventions, hidden channels, repeated reinfection, or behavior not represented in the graph, reversing the learned flow can point to the wrong source. Spectral filtering also assumes damaging noise appears as high-frequency graph variation; if important real spread is sharp or localized, filtering could remove useful evidence. The abstract does not show the details of datasets, baselines, or failure cases, and it reports average improvement without proving that every real deployment has enough continuous-time observations to support reliable inversion.

464.bp: Many organizations own graph-shaped data: users linked by interactions, products linked by purchases, patients linked by events, or accounts linked by transactions. They may want a shared learning system, but they cannot or do not want to pool all raw graph records in one place. Federated graph learning is the compromise: each client keeps its local graph, trains locally, and contributes to a global model. This paper addresses a sharper version of that setting. Client graphs are not just different in size or labels; their shapes may obey different geometric patterns. Some graphs look tree-like, with branches spreading outward. Some look flatter, where ordinary distance works. Some look more circular or clustered. FedRGL asks how a shared graph-learning system can respect those different local shapes instead of forcing every client into one fixed measuring space. The practical goal is better personalized graph learning when decentralized clients are structurally unlike one another.
464.wh: The hard part is that graph learning depends on what it means for two nodes to be near, similar, or informative neighbors. A fixed geometry quietly assumes one kind of world. In a flat space, moving twice as far roughly means twice the distance. In a branching space, small outward moves can separate many descendants quickly. In a rounded space, different routes can bend back toward one another. The abstract says existing federated graph learning methods degrade because their fixed-geometry representation space mismatches the diverse geometric structures of client data. That mismatch matters because a global model trained across clients may average together updates that were produced under incompatible distance assumptions. A second difficulty is local topology: even inside one client, the pattern of links can vary, so a single message-passing rule may copy too much information from some neighbors and too little from others. The system must share learning while preserving local graph shape.
464.naive: A smart beginner would train a graph neural network on each client, let neighboring nodes exchange information in the usual way, send model updates to a server, and average them into one global model. This is appealing because it keeps raw graph data local and gives everyone a shared learner. It fails when the clients' graphs have different shapes. If one client has a hierarchy-like graph and another has a compact community graph, the same coordinate system can distort one or both. Distorted distances make related nodes look too far apart or unrelated nodes look too close. Simple averaging then mixes lessons that do not mean the same thing geometrically, so personalization and generalization suffer.
464.ap: FedRGL's core move is to give each client a tailored geometric working space instead of demanding one universal flat map. Each client maps its local graph into a mixed-curvature product space, meaning a combined space made from flat Euclidean parts, branching hyperbolic parts, and rounded spherical parts. The client can use the mixture that better matches its own graph structure. The paper also changes how neighbor information is passed. Its Ricci-gated graph convolution uses Ricci curvature, a way of describing how local neighborhoods bend or spread, to gate the messages traveling across links. In plain terms, the model does not treat every edge as an equally trustworthy pipe. It checks the local shape around the edge and adjusts how strongly information should move. The result is personalized federated graph learning: shared training across clients, but with client-specific geometry and topology-aware message passing.
464.mech: The input is a collection of decentralized client graphs. Each client has its own nodes, edges, and local structure, and the raw graph remains on that client. First, FedRGL gives the client a personalized mixed-curvature product space. Instead of placing every node into one kind of coordinate map, it represents the graph across several geometric components: Euclidean components for flatter relations, hyperbolic components for branching or hierarchy-like relations, and spherical components for rounded or tightly cyclic relations. A node's representation is therefore a bundle of coordinates whose parts can express different shapes of nearness. Second, the local graph-learning model passes information along edges. In ordinary message passing, a node updates itself by collecting transformed signals from its neighbors. FedRGL makes that collection conditional on Ricci-style local curvature, which describes whether nearby neighborhoods expand, contract, or align around an edge. A gate uses that local shape signal to decide how much neighbor information should enter. Third, each client trains on its own graph in this tailored space and produces model updates. The federated process combines learning across clients without collecting their raw graphs. The output is a global model that has learned from multiple clients, plus personalized local behavior that better fits each client's graph geometry.
464.math: The main mathematical idea is geometry as a measuring language. A graph-learning model needs a way to turn relationships into distances and directions. Euclidean geometry is the familiar flat ruler. It works when relationships spread evenly. Hyperbolic geometry is useful for tree-like expansion because there is room for many branches to separate quickly. Spherical geometry is useful when relations are more bounded or wrap around into compact groups. A product space combines several such rulers, so the model can describe a graph whose structure is not purely one shape. The second idea is a manifold, which here means a smooth mathematical surface where local movement has a meaningful notion of distance. The abstract names Riemannian graph learning: that means learning while respecting distances on such curved surfaces rather than pretending every surface is flat. The third idea is curvature as a local diagnostic. Ricci curvature, in everyday terms, asks how neighborhoods around connected points spread compared with a baseline expectation. If two neighborhoods line up tightly, messages may be useful; if they spread apart or conflict, careless copying may mislead. The tradeoff is expressiveness versus coordination cost: richer geometry fits diverse clients, but only if training can still share useful patterns across them.
464.dots: This paper connects directly to the repo's graph-learning family, whose recurring question is how evidence should travel through links without washing away the original facts. FedRGL answers that question by making the travel rule depend on local topology and by changing the measuring space itself. It also belongs to the privacy and federated family, where the central pressure is useful cooperation across clients that cannot simply pool data. The neighboring idea is personalization: clients are not interchangeable copies, so one global average can erase local structure. Compared with recommendation, fraud, and retrieval papers that also use graphs, this paper is more focused on the geometry beneath the graph. It asks whether the map used to compare nodes is itself wrong for some clients. Compared with other federated work in the repo, its special concern is not only that client data are non-uniform, but that their graph shapes may require different kinds of distance.
464.ww: The method should help because it attacks the mismatch at the level where graph learning makes its basic judgments. If a model first places a branching graph into a flat space, later training can only partly repair the distortion. FedRGL instead gives the client a space where branching, flat, and rounded patterns can each be represented by a suitable component. That makes node closeness less arbitrary: two nodes can be close because the right part of the mixed space captures the relation that actually connects them. The Ricci-gated convolution helps for a similar reason. Neighbor averaging is useful only when a link carries relevant evidence. Some edges connect nodes whose surrounding neighborhoods support one another; other edges cross between different local structures. By letting curvature influence the gate, the model can pass strong messages where topology says the relationship is coherent and dampen messages where the neighborhood shape warns against blind smoothing. Federated training then shares what is common while leaving each client room to preserve its own structure.
464.po: The payoff claimed in the abstract is improved model accuracy and generalization across diverse geometric heterogeneity settings. In practical terms, that means a federated graph system could learn across organizations or devices whose graphs have different shapes without forcing all of them into the same flat representation. A client with hierarchy-like data, a client with compact clusters, and a client with flatter relations can each keep a better local map while still contributing to shared training. The paper's value is therefore not just higher scores; it is a more flexible way to cooperate when decentralized graph data are structurally different.
464.limits: The abstract supports the mechanism and experimental claim, but it does not prove how the system behaves in every deployment. FedRGL assumes each client's graph geometry can be usefully captured by a mixture of Euclidean, hyperbolic, and spherical components. If a graph's structure is noisy, adversarial, rapidly changing, or poorly represented by these components, the tailored space may still distort it. Ricci-based gating also assumes local curvature is a reliable clue about whether messages should pass. The abstract mentions accuracy and generalization, but not privacy leakage, communication cost, client failure, fairness across small clients, or how sensitive the method is to choosing the curvature mixture.
